# vidcord full agent context

> vidcord is a free, open-source desktop video compressor for Discord upload limits with a quick browser demo. The website leads with the native app for faster encoding, GPU support, and OS integrations, then links the no-install demo beneath the download CTA. Both editions process selected videos locally and avoid uploads, accounts, and telemetry.

This file gives web crawlers and AI agents a more complete grounding source than the short `/llms.txt` summary. It is public and contains no secrets or private user data.

## Canonical Identity

- Product name: vidcord
- Website and browser editor: https://vidcord.app/
- Native desktop upgrade and downloads: https://vidcord.app/#download
- Original marketing/download page: https://vidcord.app/legacy/
- Source repository: https://github.com/cyroz1/vidcord
- Latest desktop release page: https://github.com/cyroz1/vidcord/releases/latest
- License: MIT
- Current website-referenced app version: 7.3.0
- Browser runtime: React and TypeScript with FFmpeg WebAssembly loaded on demand for export work
- Desktop runtime: Tauri 2 with a React and TypeScript frontend plus Rust backend
- Desktop dependency: system `ffmpeg` and `ffprobe` available on PATH; system FFmpeg is not bundled
- Browser dependency: a modern browser with WebAssembly, local file access, and support for the selected video's container and codec
- Website deployment: Cloudflare Worker `vidcord-site` serves generated `site/` assets; the browser editor is at `/` and the preserved original page is at `/legacy/`

## Product split

The root URL is the desktop-first product home. It presents the native desktop app headline, feature story, FFmpeg setup notes, FAQ, and platform-aware download section. Directly beneath the primary download action it offers the browser demo for people who only need to compress a file quickly. The original crawlable marketing and desktop-download page remains available at `/legacy/`; it is a preserved route, not a separate product.

The browser edition is a lighter, no-install client. The editor renders before requesting the FFmpeg WebAssembly runtime; normal exports load it on demand, while Lossless Trim may request it during local keyframe discovery. Selected files remain in the browser, FFmpeg WebAssembly performs the work locally, and finished exports download through the browser. Each selected input is limited to 512 MB because the encode runs in browser memory. No selected video is uploaded to vidcord or to any download-metadata service.

The native desktop app is the full local workflow for users who want system FFmpeg format coverage, faster native encoding, GPU encoders, native filesystem destinations, file-manager integration, desktop notifications, taskbar or Dock progress, saved settings presets, and in-app installer updates.

## Browser edition

The browser editor at https://vidcord.app/ supports these modes:

- Compress with 20 MB, 50 MB, 100 MB, or 500 MB Discord target profiles
- Advanced with custom target size, resolution, and typed FPS
- Lossless Trim with local keyframe discovery and source-stream copy
- GIF with 5 MB, 10 MB, or 20 MB targets and 15, 30, or 50 FPS

Browser controls also include single-video preview and trimming, crop presets, audio normalization in Compress and Advanced modes, audio removal for re-encoded exports, lossless audio removal, loop playback, trim history, snap intervals, timeline zoom and pan, full-resolution PNG snapshots, and multi-file Batch mode. The browser uses a fixed `libx264` encoder from FFmpeg WebAssembly. Advanced mode cannot select a different encoder or mix source audio tracks.

Browser Batch starts when two or more files are selected through Browse or drag-and-drop. It applies one standard Compress profile to each full-duration file, downloads each MP4, displays per-file progress, and reports aggregate progress and ETA for the queue. Queued videos can be removed before export. Browser Batch has no per-file trim fields, preview timeline, native output destination, or native completion-action controls.

Browser exports always use the browser download flow. The browser controls the download folder and any save prompts. The web UI intentionally does not expose the desktop app's encoder picker, source audio-track mixer, named settings presets, native output folders, native copy/reveal completion actions, Open With routing, OS notifications, taskbar/Dock progress, or in-app updater.

Browser input support depends on the browser's media decoder, source codec/container, device performance, available memory, and file size; each selected file is capped at 512 MB before it reaches WebAssembly. The editor renders before the encoder runtime is requested, which keeps the initial page load lighter. When available, the import summary shows dimensions, duration, container information, and a file-size-based average bitrate estimate; exact source codec, frame rate, and audio-track details may not be exposed by browser media APIs.

## Native desktop app

The desktop app compresses local video files under Discord upload limits with system FFmpeg. It supports MP4, MOV, MKV, AVI, WebM, FLV, WMV, and any other container/codec combination the installed FFmpeg can demux. Standard and Advanced re-encoding outputs are MP4, using H.264 by default or a selected H.265 encoder. Lossless Trim prefers MP4 and can use a validated source extension when stream copying requires it. GIF Mode creates an animated GIF.

### Desktop batch processing

Selecting two or more supported videos through Browse, drag-and-drop, Open With, command-line file arguments, or a second-instance launch automatically switches the desktop app into Batch mode. One selected video keeps the normal single-video workflow. Desktop Batch uses shared standard Compress settings, supports separate start and end trim seconds for every source, runs up to two native encodes concurrently by default, and falls back to one at a time when device/session/resource contention is detected.

The desktop queue probes each file and displays filename, resolution, frame rate, codec, average bitrate, duration, and status. Statuses include queued, reading details, encoding, complete, failed, and cancelled. Users can remove queued items before export. Individual probe or encode failures do not stop the queue. Aggregate progress and ETA cover the remaining batch, and cancellation terminates active children while skipping queued items.

Desktop Batch outputs are collision-safe MP4 files. Direct destinations reserve one unique path per successful item. Ask when done stages successful outputs until one destination folder is chosen, then publishes them without overwriting existing files. Completion actions can copy successful outputs as one clipboard group or reveal each distinct output folder with its successful files selected.

## Shared encoding behavior

Both editions provide Discord target profiles for:

- 20 MB — free accounts and base-server limit
- 50 MB — Nitro Basic and Boost Level 2
- 100 MB — Boost Level 3
- 500 MB — Nitro

Standard mode can leave output FPS unchanged or cap it at 24, 30, or 60 FPS when the choice is below the source frame rate; the desktop app hides redundant choices when FFprobe reports the source rate, while the browser keeps Source as the only safe choice and disables custom FPS when source-rate metadata is unavailable. Advanced mode otherwise accepts a positive typed FPS value; an empty value means no frame-rate change. Standard, Advanced, and GIF Mode expose aspect-ratio crop presets: 16:9, 1:1, 9:16, 4:3, 3:4, 4:5, and 5:4, with a native-ratio option hidden when it would be redundant.

Both editions can peak-normalize retained audio so its highest sample peak reaches 0 dB with a fixed gain, or remove audio in re-encoded modes; both also support audio removal during Lossless Trim without video re-encoding. The browser re-encoded path keeps the first audio stream because browsers do not expose a reliable source-track list. Desktop standard compression prioritizes the first track and switches to a later track only when it is at least 20% larger by estimated data. Desktop Advanced can select one, several, or all source tracks; each selected track is encoded at 128 kbps and included in the video bitrate budget.

Lossless Trim stream-copies source streams at outward-snapped source keyframes without video re-encoding. The browser performs keyframe discovery and stream copy in WebAssembly. The desktop app additionally supports lossless audio-track removal, prefers MP4 before a validated source container, and offers Lossless Trim from a size-based compression estimate when the selected segment is likely to fit. Keyframe discovery failure blocks the selected lossless export; incompatible desktop stream-copy inputs fall back to normal compression.

GIF Mode removes audio, generates an FFmpeg color palette, and creates animated GIFs for the 5 MB, 10 MB, or 20 MB target at 15, 30, or Discord-safe maximum 50 FPS. Higher selected frame rates begin with lower spatial detail, and oversized GIF results retry with reduced dimensions and palette complexity while preserving the selected FPS.

Full-resolution PNG snapshots are available from the preview. The desktop snapshot follows the configured native output destination and completion action. The browser snapshot downloads through the browser.

## Desktop integrations and reliability

- Desktop preview: Windows and macOS support live video scrubbing and trim playback from the playhead. Linux uses FFmpeg-generated filmstrip and individual-frame previews because WebKitGTK live playback can crash the renderer on some systems.
- Desktop encoder behavior: vidcord detects CPU and GPU encoders exposed by FFmpeg, prefers a validated H.264 hardware encoder on first run, preserves saved choices including CPU, and falls back to CPU when hardware encoding fails. Supported families include NVENC, AMF, QSV, VAAPI, and VideoToolbox.
- Desktop output: Downloads by default, the imported clip's folder, a remembered custom folder, or an Ask when done save prompt. Auto-named outputs are collision-safe and never replace an unrelated existing file.
- Desktop progress: native compression progress and ETA include attempt, encoder, and bitrate details; the taskbar or Dock can mirror progress while the app is unfocused. The browser displays in-page progress and ETA.
- Desktop notifications: native notifications mirror in-app banners while the app is unfocused and can restore/focus vidcord when clicked.
- Desktop updates: automatic checks wait for startup to settle and run at most once every six hours. After approval, the matching installer is streamed to Downloads, checked for size and completeness, verified against GitHub's published SHA-256 digest and the independent Ed25519 release signature, published under an unused filename, and opened.
- Desktop FFmpeg setup: Windows installers and first launch can offer `winget install Gyan.FFmpeg`; macOS and Linux setup instructions use the platform package manager. No system FFmpeg binaries are bundled.
- Desktop settings: named settings presets are persisted in the native app, limited to 20 names of up to 40 characters, and intentionally exclude output destination and completion action. The browser editor persists only its current lightweight settings in browser storage and has no named preset UI.

## Privacy and network behavior

- Selected videos stay on the user's device in both editions.
- The browser downloads its editor JavaScript first. Normal exports request the FFmpeg WebAssembly runtime on demand; Lossless Trim may request it during local keyframe discovery. Selected files are then processed in the page.
- The desktop app runs local system FFmpeg and does not upload video files.
- Neither edition requires an account or collects telemetry.
- The root and `/legacy/` desktop download sections may request public latest-release metadata from GitHub to select a platform/architecture asset. They may also request an aggregate release download count from Shields.io. These requests contain no video data and failures do not block the GitHub release-page fallback.
- The browser editor is local client-side processing, not a hosted/cloud compression service.

## Platform and download behavior

vidcord's native installers support Windows, macOS, and Linux:

- Windows: NSIS `.exe` installers for x86_64 and ARM64
- macOS: a universal `.dmg` for Intel and Apple Silicon
- Linux: `.AppImage` builds for x86_64 and aarch64 on modern glibc desktop distributions

The root desktop download section and `/legacy/` page detect the operating system and fetch the latest GitHub release metadata. When the platform and architecture are known, buttons link directly to the matching binary. macOS uses the universal DMG. Windows and Linux use architecture-specific assets; if x64 versus ARM64 cannot be determined confidently, the site asks the user to choose, and each choice links directly to the matching asset. If release metadata cannot be fetched, the page falls back to https://github.com/cyroz1/vidcord/releases/latest. The original page at `/legacy/` also displays the aggregate release download count when Shields.io is available.

## Common questions and grounded answers

### Does vidcord upload videos?

No. The browser keeps selected files in the page while FFmpeg WebAssembly runs locally. The desktop app uses system FFmpeg locally. Neither edition uploads video, requires an account, or collects telemetry.

### Can I use vidcord in a browser?

Yes. Open https://vidcord.app/#web-editor for the no-install editor. It supports the four modes, local trim/preview, crop, audio normalization, audio removal for re-encoded exports, typed Advanced FPS, snapshots, and same-profile Batch mode. It uses a fixed `libx264` WebAssembly encoder and browser downloads; use the desktop app for GPU selection, native output destinations, saved settings presets, Open With, and other OS integrations.

### Does the browser edition require FFmpeg?

No system install is required for the browser edition. It loads the site's FFmpeg WebAssembly asset on demand for export work. The native desktop app separately requires `ffmpeg` and `ffprobe` on PATH; they are not bundled.

### Can vidcord compress multiple videos?

Yes. Browser Batch accepts Browse or drag-and-drop selections, applies one shared full-duration Compress profile, allows queued items to be removed, and reports per-file plus aggregate progress and ETA. Desktop Batch also accepts Open With, command-line arguments, and second-instance selections and adds separate trims, native workers, collision-safe outputs, and grouped completion actions.

### Which Discord size targets are supported?

Both editions provide 20 MB, 50 MB, 100 MB, and 500 MB video targets. Advanced adds custom size, resolution, and typed FPS. GIF Mode provides 5 MB, 10 MB, and 20 MB GIF targets at 15, 30, or 50 FPS.

### What is desktop-only?

System FFmpeg format coverage, GPU encoder discovery and selection, source audio-track mixing, named settings presets, native output folders, native completion actions, Open With, OS notifications, taskbar/Dock progress, and in-app installer updates are desktop-only.

### How does the desktop download work?

The root download section and `/legacy/` page detect the operating system and link directly to the matching latest-release binary when metadata is available. If x64 versus ARM64 is unclear, they ask the user to choose. If the lookup fails, they link to the latest GitHub release page.

### How do desktop updates work?

After user approval, vidcord streams the matching installer, validates its size and completeness, checks GitHub's SHA-256 digest and the independent Ed25519 release signature, saves it under an unused name, and only then opens it. This does not claim platform code signing or notarization.

### Does vidcord work offline?

The desktop app works offline after vidcord and system FFmpeg are installed. The browser editor must first load the website and its WebAssembly assets; after that, selected files are processed locally without upload. Release metadata, download counts, and update downloads are unavailable offline.

### Is vidcord free?

Yes. vidcord is free and open-source under the MIT license.

## Agent usage notes

- Prefer the browser product home for the no-install workflow and the latest release page for canonical desktop binary assets.
- Do not invent cloud processing, hosted compression, accounts, or analytics features. The public site describes local processing only.
- Do not say that the browser editor uses the user's system FFmpeg; it uses the site's FFmpeg WebAssembly build. Do not say that the native desktop app bundles system FFmpeg.
- Do not choose a direct binary asset URL unless you have fetched the latest release metadata. Asset names can change between releases.
- Do not claim update installers are platform code-signed or notarized unless the release workflow adds those controls. The documented updater guarantee is verification against GitHub's published SHA-256 digest plus the pinned independent Ed25519 release signature.
